newsitem.title: USA: UPS-Teamsters clash not bellwether in part-timer issue.
newsitem.headline: UPS-Teamsters clash not bellwether in part-timer issue.

text.p: Teamsters President Ron Carey has worked hard to cast his union's battle with United Parcel Service of America Inc. as a broader fight for the rights of workers not to have their full-time jobs relegated to part-time piece work.
It's a message that strikes a chord with a work force often anxious about the next round of corporate downsizings and restructurings and fearful of losing the benefits that accompany full-time work.

But a number of labour and management experts alike agree that while Carey may have renewed a national dialogue on the trend, the UPS-Teamsters confrontation is unlikely to become a bellwether event in the part-time versus full-time labour issue, no matter what the ultimate outcome of the strike.

"It's certainly resonating," said Greg Tarpinian, executive director of the Labour Research Association, a union-backed think tank in New York. "But will it advance or reverse the trend? No, I don't think so."
The walkout by 185,000 union members entered its seventh day on Sunday.
"Carey is just latching on to an anxiety trend," said David Thompson, workplace counsel for the Small Business Survival Committee, a Washington lobbying group.
About 23.2 million Americans hold part-time jobs, accounting for 18.3 percent of the nation's total work force of more than 126 million, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labour Statistics.

With the nation's unemployment rate continuing at near-record lows, the current use of part-time workers is down from a recent high in 1994 of 23.3 million part-time workers, or 18.9 percent of the total.
The experts say UPS' use of part-time workers is not reflective of their use in other sectors.

It bears no resemblance, for instance, to the pattern in retailing, the largest employer of part-time help, said George Paajanen, vice president of Personnel Decisions International, a Minneapolis-based staffing consultancy.

The world's largest shipping company employs part-timers for a few hours a day to cover crunch processing and delivery periods for which it makes no economic sense to hire full-time staff. In retailing, where Paajanen said up to 90 percent of workers are part-time, non-career employees, companies make deliberate efforts not to hire more costly full-time staff.

"The part-time issue at UPS is so different from the trend, it just doesn't apply," agreed the Small Business Survival Committee's Thompson, noting that UPS part-timers are covered by the union. "This isn't the example."
Still, some say the outcome of so high-profile a conflict will be influential, particularly if UPS management prevails.
Georgetown University professor of labour relations Douglas McCabe says plenty of corporate executives will take their cue from UPS if it forces Carey to back down on the part-timers isssue.
"This is a strategic issue for them, and company executives will follow the outcome," McCabe said. "They will take the ball and run with it."
